title: Realtime: WebSockets, SSE and polling
tagline: Push updates to clients the moment they happen, and know which server holds which connection.
why:
HTTP is request and response: the server cannot speak until the client asks. Chat messages, a driver's location, a voucher turning "redeemed" on the merchant's screen, or tokens streaming from an LLM all need the server to push.

There are four ways to do it, and they trade simplicity for latency and cost. The interesting part is not the protocol but the fleet: a long-lived connection pins a user to one gateway server, so when a message for user B arrives somewhere else, you need to know where B is connected and get the message there.
how:
The four options.

  • Short polling. The client asks every few seconds. Trivial and works through any proxy, but most requests return nothing, and the delay is up to the interval. 1M clients polling every 5 s is 200,000 requests a second.
  • Long polling. The server holds the request open until there is news or ~30 s pass, then the client asks again. Near-instant delivery over plain HTTP, but every message costs a new request.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE). One HTTP response that never ends (text/event-stream). Server to client only; the browser reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID so you can resume. Great for feeds, notifications and LLM token streams.
  • WebSockets. An HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket is answered with 101 Switching Protocols, and the same TCP connection then carries WebSocket frames in both directions. Small frames both ways; best for chat, games, collaborative editing and live location.

The gateway fleet. Clients connect through a load balancer to stateless-ish gateway servers whose only job is holding sockets. Business logic lives in normal services behind them. Each gateway handles tens of thousands of mostly idle connections.

Connection registry. When a socket opens, the gateway writes user:B → gw2 to Redis with a TTL it refreshes on every heartbeat. To reach B, a service looks B up.

Pub/sub fan-out. Services publish to a channel (per gateway, per user or per room) on Redis pub/sub, NATS or Kafka. Each gateway subscribes to the channels for the users it holds and writes the message to their sockets. Pub/sub is usually fire-and-forget, so persist the message first; a client that reconnects asks for everything after the last id it saw.

Keepalives and reconnects. Send a ping every 20 to 30 s so load balancers and NATs do not drop idle connections. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, because a gateway deploy or crash drops thousands of sockets at once.

steps.note: Client A sends an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket and its auth token. The load balancer must allow upgrades and an idle timeout longer than the heartbeat interval.
The gateway checks the token and answers 101 Switching Protocols. From now on this TCP connection is pinned to gateway 1.
Gateway 1 registers user:A → gw1 in Redis with a TTL of about 60 s, refreshed on each 25 s heartbeat. If the gateway dies, the entry expires by itself.
Client B connects the same way, and the load balancer happens to pick gateway 2.
Gateway 2 accepts. Most of its sockets are idle most of the time: memory per connection, not CPU, sets how many fit on one box.
user:B → gw2. A user on two devices has two entries.
A sends a frame on its open socket with a client-generated message id, so a retry after a dropped connection is not stored twice.
It arrives at gateway 1, which only holds sockets and forwards to the service.
The chat service validates the message and stores it first. Pub/sub may drop messages; the database is how B catches up later.
Look up B: connected to gw2. If there is no entry, B is offline: send a push notification instead.
Publish to the channel for gateway 2 (or for user B).
Gateway 2 is subscribed to its channel and receives the message in a millisecond or two.
Gateway 2 writes the frame to B's socket.
B sees it, end to end typically under 100 ms. B acks the message id so the server can mark it delivered.

flows.name: Room fan-out
flows.desc: One message, members on many gateways.

steps.note: A posts to room 42, which has members connected to many gateways.
Publish once to channel room:42. The service does not need to know who is online where.
Every gateway that holds a member of room 42 is subscribed to that channel, including gateway 1 for A's other devices.
Gateway 2 gets it too and writes it to each local member's socket. For a room with 100k members, this fan-out is the expensive part: batch it and rate limit it.
Delivered down the existing socket.
If B was offline, B fetches everything after its last seen message id on reconnect.

tradeoffs.pro: Simplest; works through every proxy and caches; no connection state on the server.
tradeoffs.con: Wasteful (most responses are empty) and latency is up to the polling interval.

tradeoffs.pro: Near-instant delivery over plain HTTP; good fallback when WebSockets are blocked.
tradeoffs.con: A new request per message or timeout; holding many requests open still needs an async server.

tradeoffs.pro: Plain HTTP, built-in reconnect and resume with Last-Event-ID; ideal for one-way streams like feeds and LLM tokens.
tradeoffs.con: Server to client only (client sends with normal requests); text only; on HTTP/1.1 counts against the browser's ~6 connections per host.

tradeoffs.pro: Full duplex with tiny per-message overhead; best for chat, live location and collaboration.
tradeoffs.con: Stateful connections: needs a gateway fleet, a registry, heartbeats, reconnect logic and careful deploys.

numbers: Polling cost: 1M clients every 5 s = 200,000 req/s, almost all returning nothing.
One tuned gateway holds roughly 50k to 100k mostly idle sockets; memory per connection is in the tens of KB. 1M concurrent users ≈ 10 to 20 gateways.
Heartbeat every 20 to 30 s. AWS ALB's default idle timeout is 60 s; an idle socket with no pings is silently cut.
WebSocket frame header: 2 to 14 bytes, versus hundreds of bytes of headers for each polling request.
Redis pub/sub delivery inside one region: about 1 ms. A gateway restart with 50k sockets means 50k reconnects: spread them with jittered backoff over 10 to 30 s.
say: For two-way realtime I'll use WebSockets through a gateway fleet that only holds connections; business logic stays in stateless services behind it.
Each gateway registers user-to-gateway in Redis with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats, and services publish to the right gateway's channel over pub/sub.
Messages are persisted before they are published, so a client that reconnects asks for everything after its last seen id and nothing is lost if pub/sub drops one.
pitfalls: Treating pub/sub as durable. Redis pub/sub drops messages for subscribers that are not connected. Persist first, and let clients resync by last seen id.
Keeping business logic and state in the gateway. Then a deploy or crash loses work, and you cannot scale sockets and logic separately.
No heartbeats. Load balancers and mobile NATs cut idle connections; the server keeps writing into a dead socket and thinks the user is online.
Clients that reconnect immediately on failure. One gateway restart becomes a reconnect storm that knocks over the next gateway. Use exponential backoff with jitter.
Reaching for WebSockets when SSE or polling would do. A dashboard that refreshes every 30 s does not need a stateful connection fleet.

quiz.q: You need to stream LLM tokens to a browser. The client sends one prompt and then only receives. What is the simplest good fit?
options: Long polling with a new request per token
quiz.why: SSE is one-way server push over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnect. The prompt goes in a normal POST. WebSockets work but add state you do not need, and long polling pays a new request for every token.

quiz.q: User B is connected to gateway 7. A message for B is handled by a service instance that has no socket for B. How does it reach B?
options: The load balancer forwards it to B
Look up B in the connection registry and publish to gateway 7's channel
quiz.why: The registry maps users to gateways; pub/sub carries the message to the gateway that owns the socket. The load balancer has no idea which socket belongs to B.

quiz.q: After a gateway crash, 50,000 clients reconnect within one second and overload the remaining gateways. What fixes it?
options: Exponential backoff with random jitter on the client
quiz.why: Jitter spreads reconnects over many seconds so the fleet absorbs them. Without it, every client retries at the same moment.

quiz.q: Why persist a chat message before publishing it to pub/sub?
options: Pub/sub is slower than the database
It is required by the WebSocket protocol
To reduce memory on the gateway
Pub/sub may drop it, and an offline receiver needs a durable copy
quiz.why: Redis pub/sub does not keep messages for absent subscribers. The database is the source of truth; the push is only a fast path.
